english-1.title: Passage I
english-1.html:
A Small Rescue

While surveying a wooded campground near Helena, Montana, for damaged trees, a team of forestry workers discovered two baby Western screech owls. Nestled in a1 cardboard box lined with blankets and pine boughs,1 the birds were delivered to me, a wildlife rehabilitator with Big Sky Bird Rescue.

The two-week-old owlets were weak and dehydrated when they arrived at the rescue center. Under my care, though,2 the birds enjoyed a steady diet of crickets and mice, quickly becoming bright-eyed and tripling in weight. When their flight feathers started coming in, Lila and Twyla, playfully named by the forestry workers, were moved from a refuge for very young owls3 to a spacious outdoor enclosure.

There, the owls gained experience running, flapping their wings, hunting various prey, and flying. [4] They chased mice and flew easily to catch crickets. Most importantly, they began to show appropriate defensive actions toward humans, such as clacking their beaks and hissing. Alert and confident, the ten-week-old owls would be able to survive independently; doing so without5 a defensive mother—or a devoted naturalist—to feed and protect them.

english-2.title: Passage Ii
english-2.html:
The Musical Made Modern

When the musical Oklahoma! opened on Broadway in 1943, from the outset,6 it was an immediate success. The show went on to become one of the most profitable and critically lauded musicals in modern history. The success came as a surprise to its creators, composer Richard Rodgers and lyricist Oscar Hammerstein II.

The composers of Oklahoma!7, who chose to break from the strictures of traditional theater. Historically, musicals had taken the form of “revues” with no coherent plot, or “through-line,” that played out over the course of the show. Meanwhile,8 musicals featured loose collections of narratively unrelated love songs, usually sung by a male and a female lead. In addition, they included chorus lines of women who danced and sang but were not characters in the show.

In Oklahoma! every song served an overarching story, and everyone who appeared on stage, had a single9 role to play,9 in the drama. Each actor was in character throughout; each song explored the relationships and conflicts between characters. In a number of ways— some striking and some subtle—this musical redecorated10 American musical theater forever.

english-3.title: Passage Iii
english-3.html:
Schmandt-Besserat and Ancient Accounting

During a 1929 excavation, of the ancient city of Uruk,11 located in present-day Iraq, archaeologists unearthed clay tablets inscribed with wedge-shaped writing. The writing was identified as proto-cuneiform. Dating back to 3100 BCE, this writing seemed indecipherable. Also at Uruk, archaeologists found shaped clay objects, each measuring only a12 few centimeters, molded into shapes such as13 cones, discs, and cylinders. These artifacts were also a mystery; no one knew how or why they were used.

By the 1970s, hundreds of the tiny, enigmatic objects had been found throughout the Middle East. Archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat was traveling to various museums throughout four continents,14 cataloging the objects, when she made a connection. Other, more recent groups used small objects to record the numbers of animals and amounts of grain exchanged in business transactions. Such information led Schmandt-Besserat to determine that the Uruk objects, which she began calling “tokens,” had been used to count goods. Each token represented one commodity, such as one lamb or one loaf of bread. Using a one-to-one counting method, so that15 someone had five jars of oil, he or she would also have five ovoid tokens representing those jars. As the people of Uruk bought, sold, and traded goods, some were16 exchanged for record-keeping purposes.

Furthermore, Schmandt-Besserat realized that with the proto-cuneiform on the Uruk tablets resembled17 indentations of tokens. In addition to keeping track of goods via tokens, the people of Uruk kept records on the tablets. The first tablet recordings were made by pressing tokens into the tablets while the clay was still wet. Eventually, the people of Uruk began using a stylus to etch the shapes of indentations rather than creating actual impressions.

Schmandt-Besserat shed light on the mystery of the tokens and provided an interpretation of the proto-cuneiform tablets. In doing so,18 she has helped archaeologists better understand the origins19 of counting, accounting, and writing.

english-4.title: Passage Iv
english-4.html:
The Iron Man of Charleston

Only nine years old,21 Philip Simmons first walked passed22 the busy blacksmith’s shop on his way to school in Charleston, South Carolina, he was captivated. Furnaces blazed, hammers clanged, and sparks flew—especially for Simmons. From that moment, he saw ironwork as his calling. Four years later, in 1925, the shop owner offered him an apprenticeship. He plunged in,23 quickly gaining skill at the craft.

[1] Unfortunately, just as Simmons was learning his trade, the demand for blacksmiths was in fast decline. [2] To make money, Simmons had to adapt—by becoming an artist of iron. [3] Automobiles had undercut the market for horseshoes; factories were mass-producing parts previously forged by hand. [24]

Decorative ironwork was already prominent in the streets of Charleston, hundreds of gates, fences, and25 railings25 featured curves, curlicues, and other flourishes. Bending and beating iron into graceful shapes are never26 easy to do, but Simmons mastered it. Soon his work surpassed the quality of the city’s older pieces.

Moreover, Simmons broadened the cultural scope of Charleston’s ironwork. The city’s iron pieces had historically reflected European design, and Simmons excelled in that style. But his mentor, whom,27 like Simmons, was African American, also exposed him to a centuries-old West African ironworking tradition. Both Simmons’s approach to his craft and his use of innovative design elements [28] suggest the influences of that tradition.

In a career lasting nearly eight decades, Simmons gained renown for his skill and originality. Greatly inspired by nature, he insisted that his leaves and animals appear “live.” On his gates, snakes seem ready to strike; egrets appear about to take flight. He would tell his own apprentices that although29 nature doesn’t make two leaves exactly alike, they couldn’t either. Eventually earning the highest honors bestowed on American artists, Simmons kept ironwork artistry alive and thriving throughout the streets of Charleston.

english-5.title: Passage V
english-5.html:
Zadar’s Sea Organ

As I step off the ferry onto the Riva promenade in Zadar, Croatia, I spot them—seven sets of long concrete steps that descend into the sea. Stretching for over two hundred feet along the curve of the coast, the steps are awash31 with people strolling or sunbathing, waiting for sunset. With gentle waves breaking against the lower steps, the cordial, serene mood envelops me.

The scene is lovely, but I’ve seen lovely places32 before.32 Below the murmuring voices and lapping water, the haunting tones of Zadar’s Sea Organ resonate in my chest like whale song. Despite years studying33 this instrument’s design, I’m still surprised by what I hear in person. The music is nothing like the bright, resounding chords that fill cathedrals. These chords are slightly atonal, actually, and unexpectedly soothing. Today, there’s also a natural rhythm to the music—much like the rocking of a boat, with the lower and higher notes—34alternating in volume as if on a sonic seesaw.

[35] Hidden below the steps are thirty-five organ-like pipes of various lengths. When waves meet the shore, they propel air through the pipes and out vertical slots in the top steps, generating a spectral array of sounds.

What’s so masterful about this organ, though, is how carefully its designer, Nikola Bašíc, accounted for the randomness of nature. In other organs, creating resonant, harmonious chords requires36 constant control over how forcefully air is pushed through the pipes. But there’s no consistency to the force of waves: some pound the shore; some just tickle it. The Sea Organ’s design—from the pipe’s37 spacing to which pitches they produce—not only accounts for that inconsistency but fully embraces it.

In the wake of a passing barge,38 the pipes to my left suddenly grow much more loudly, their39 higher pitches nearly drowning out those on my right. Yet the overall effect doesn’t change. The airy, round tones still twine with the lapping of the waves. Calming40 my thoughts and buoying my spirits.

english-6.title: Passage Vi
english-6.html:
Make Our Blocks Super

Living in a city can come with excitement41 and opportunity—41and with noise pollution, feelings of isolation, and little access to green space. Some people are able to overlook these drawbacks.42 To alleviate them, US officials should look to a novel concept being implemented in Barcelona, Spain.

In the early 2000s, this densely populated city began piloting the superblock: an area of three blocks by three blocks in which most automobile traffic is prohibited,43 from interior streets. The concept, proposed by urbanist Salvador Rueda, allows those streets to become “pedestrian first,” prioritizing access for walkers and cyclists. Ideally, superblocks also include amenities that encourage residents to congregate outside, such as benches, green space, and playgrounds. Eventually, city planners hope to install over44 five hundred superblocks throughout Barcelona.44

With thoughtful, collaborative planning, officials should be able to tackle any hurdles connected with45 implementing superblocks in the United States. For example, while it may take creativity to design superblocks in cities that weren’t laid out in a grid, the principle of increasing space for pedestrians by limiting vehicles can be applied with or without a traditional grid. Also, when46 there would be associated costs, installing superblocks requires no significant reconstruction of existing roads, so cities could likely pilot a program with minimal investment. Finally, to address logistics such as parking and deliveries, officials, working closely with residents,47 to draft a plan that best meets their needs. [48]

[A] Barcelona residents have largely embraced superblocks, and many report greater satisfaction with their neighborhoods after a superblock installation. [B] Inspired by Barcelona’s success, officials in several other European cities are piloting similar designs,49 and US officials should do the same. [C] Superblocks will be worth the investment of time and money to increase the quality of life in our cities. [D] [50]

Passage A by Anousheh Ansari

I immigrated to the United States from Iran, a
teenager who didn’t speak a word of English. Growing
up in Iran, my head was always in the clouds. At night
I would spend hours watching the stars, wanting
nothing more than to become an astronaut, to fly to
space and touch them. My mind was filled with a future
where starships would fly to every corner of the
universe. I would be the science officer aboard the
Starship Enterprise, traveling through wormholes and
exploring strange new worlds and new civilizations—to
boldly go where no one has gone before. I dreamed of a
future with time machines, parallel universes,
teleportation and a United Federation of Planets. I was
fascinated by all these possibilities because when
you’re a child, everything is possible—there are no
boundaries, and everything is a puzzle to be solved,
every dark corner an opportunity for discovery.
When I arrived in the United States, the realities
of life put me on a completely different path. I went to
school and studied electrical engineering while working
full-time. My family moved to the United States with
nothing but hopes for a new life and a better future, so
finding a job to support myself and my family was
important. I found a job at a major telecommunications
company, MCI, and started my career as an engineer.
Working at MCI was a great experience—I learned the
ins and outs of the corporate world while learning a lot
about the telecom industry.
President Roosevelt once said: “Far better it is to
dare mighty things, to win glorious triumphs, even
though checkered by failure, than to rank with those
timid spirits who neither enjoy nor suffer much,
because they live in the gray twilight that knows
neither victory nor defeat.” I like to believe that’s how
I live my life, and so, a few years later, after meeting
my husband at MCI, we both left the company and
started on our road to entrepreneurship.
Building a company from scratch and growing it is
exciting, but also a big challenge.

Passage B by Ellen Ullman

The author, in 1979, had just purchased a TRS-80
microcomputer.
Computer programming was something I had
never done before and had never even imagined trying.
Yet I had a cocky courage and went ahead, armed
with little but some knowledge about video, the
understanding that I was not afraid of machines, and an
honors thesis on Macbeth.
Naturally, I began by thrashing around. The
programming was done in the BASIC coding language,
which is easy to learn if you stick to easy things, like
getting text to appear on the screen, a black -and-white
TV that was old technology even then. However,
writing an actual program, coding a set of statements
that did what you intended them to do, was another
matter.
For the first two months, I was maddened,
indignant at the machine’s opacity, ashamed at my own
ignorance. I stayed up nights. I forgot to eat.
Afternoons found me in my pajamas. I was still a day
laborer in those days, a temp, filing papers, answering
switchboards, pumping gas and wiping windshields at a
gas-only station—I had to make money somehow. But I
turned away all offers for employment. I was not
available: I was somewhere deep in a tangle code.
I fell into the traps early BASIC laid all around
you. You could jump around in the code. You could
GOTO here and GOTO here and GOSUB there, until it
was hard to keep track of where you had come from or
where to go next. All the variables were “visible”
everywhere, not confined to specific blocks of code, so
it was easy to step on your values unwittingly. I didn’t
understand that the GOTOs were traps. Only later did I
learn that early BASIC was called spaghetti code for its
mess of strands. For me, though, at first, it was more
like a pile of entwined hissing snakes.
I began to chip away at the confines of my
ignorance. I moved from failure to failure, which,
perversely, proved alluring. By “perverse” I mean the
sort of experience that drags you into the unknown and
abandons you there, and where, against all expectation,
you find you like being. In other words, fun.
The snakes turned into lines and arrows drawn on
a piece of paper, the variables into a list of line
numbers where they were referenced. I told myself if I
could follow the flows of time in Macbeth—where the
past kept being mistaken for the future, as perceived
time rolled backward and forward, with a singular
startling moment in the present, when Macbeth kills the
king—well, all these code tangles were nothing.
When I got my first decent little program running
(graphs using x’s to show the decreasing amplitudes of
a bouncing ball), I sat back with a pleasure that
reminded me of the time I’d fixed a carburetor: It
works.

reading-2.title: Passage Ii
reading-2.html:
INFORMATIONAL: This passage is from the article “Our Brain Typically Overlooks This Brilliant Problem-Solving Strategy” by Diana Kwon (©2021 by Scientific American). Graphic is adapted from the article “People Systematically Overlook Subtractive Changes” by Gabrielle S. Adams et al. (©2021 by Nature).

Leidy Klotz, an engineer at the University of
Virginia, noticed that minimalist designs, in which
elements are removed from an existing model, were
uncommon. So he reached out to Gabrielle Adams, a
social psychologist at the university, to try to figure out
why this was the case. The two researchers
hypothesized that there might be a psychological
explanation: when faced with a problem, people tend to
select solutions that involve adding new elements
rather than taking existing components away.
Adams, Klotz and their colleagues set out to test if
their hunch was correct. “We wanted to investigate
whether, and to what extent, people actually
overlooked subtraction when they’re tasked with
changing things,” Adams says. Their investigation
“wasn’t literature driven, because there’s [no academic]
literature on this phenomenon. It was really just us
putting our heads together to think up why this might
be the case.”
The researchers first carried out a set of
observational studies, assessments without a control
group, to see whether this bias existed at all. In one,
they asked 91 participants to make a pattern
symmetrical by either adding or removing colored
boxes. Only 18 people (20 percent) used subtraction. In
another, the team scanned through an archive of ideas
for improvement submitted to an incoming university
president and found that only 11 percent of 651
proposals involved eliminating an existing regulation,
practice or program. Similar results emerged across
tasks that involved modifying structures, essays and
itineraries—in each case, the vast majority of people
chose to augment rather than remove.
To determine why people tended to choose
additive solutions, the team dug deeper by conducting a
series of eight experiments with more than
1,500 individuals recruited either from a university
campus or through Amazon Mechanical Turk, a
crowdsourcing Web site. In one experiment, people
were asked to stabilize the roof of a Lego structure held
up by a single block that rested atop a cube-shaped
base. The reward for completing the task was $1, and
participants could add new blocks for 10 cents apiece
or get rid of blocks for free. The researchers wrote that
one group was provided a cue about potential
subtractive solutions by being told, “Each piece that
you add costs ten cents but removing pieces is free,”
while another group was just told, “Each piece that you
add costs ten cents.” Almost two thirds of people in the
cued group ended up choosing to eliminate the single
block rather than adding new ones, compared with
41 percent of those who had not received the prompt.
The researchers also observed that people were
more likely to remove features when they were given
more opportunities to consider alternative ways to
address a problem: when participants were asked to
create a symmetrical pattern by adding or eliminating
colored blocks, they opted for removal more often if
they were given practice trials than if they had just one
chance to tackle the problem. On the other hand,
having to simultaneously juggle another task—such as
keeping track of numbers on a screen—made
individuals less likely to subtract elements to solve the
same problem, suggesting that it requires more effort to
think up subtractive solutions than additive ones. (In
both of these experiments, removing blocks was the
more efficient solution.)
These findings, which were published in Nature,
suggest that “additive solutions have sort of a
privileged status—they tend to come to mind quickly
and easily,” says Benjamin Converse, a social
psychologist at the University of Virginia and a
co-author of the study. “Subtractive solutions are not
necessarily harder to consider, but they take more
effort to find.”
The authors “convincingly demonstrate that we
tend to not consider subtractive solutions as much as
additive ones,” says Tom Meyvis, a consumer
psychologist at New York University, who was not
directly involved in the study but reviewed it and
co-authored a commentary about it in Nature.

reading-3.title: Passage Iii
reading-3.html:
INFORMATIONAL: This passage is from the book Naturalist by Edward O. Wilson (©1994 by Island Press). The full name of the colleague the author mentions throughout the passage is William L. Brown.

Subspecies were (and still are) given formal
latinized names by taxonomists. The bald eagle
Haliaeetus leucocephalus, for example, is a species
divided by taxonomists into two such races, the
southern bald eagle Haliaeetus leucocephalus
leucocephalus and the northern bald eagle Haliaeetus
leucocephalus washingtoniensis.
For reasons not immediately clear to Brown and
me, subspecies seemed insubstantial and arbitrary. We
set out to conduct a critical review of the premises
behind their recognition, by looking at real cases. The
foundations proved even weaker than we had imagined.
We discovered that the geographic limits of subspecies
are often hard or impossible to draw, because the traits
used to define them vary in a discordant pattern. The
nature of the discordance can be most immediately
understood with an imaginary but typical example:
color in a butterfly species varies east to west, size
decreases from north to south, and an extra band
appears on the hind wing in a few localities near the
center. And so on for any number of traits the
taxonomist might choose from an almost endless list
available for classification. It follows that the identity
of the subspecies into which the butterfly species is
divided depends on the traits chosen to define them.
Pick color, and you have two east–west races. Pick
color plus size, and four races in a quadrant come into
existence. Add the hind-wing band, and the number of
races can double again. Hence the subspecies are
arbitrary. In 1953 we published a report recommending
that subspecies not be given formal names. We argued
that the geographic variation is real all right but should
instead be analyzed trait by trait. It is more informative
to focus on the traits and not on the subspecies that
might be concocted from them.
Our critique of the subspecies triggered a tempest
of controversy in the journals of systematic biology.
When the debate subsided several years later, opinion
had shifted to our side. Fewer triple-name races were
formally described thereafter, and emphasis was
increasingly placed on the properties of independently
varying traits. Nevertheless, I realize now that Brown
and I overstated our case in 1953. Some populations
can be defined clearly with sets of genetic traits that do
change in a concordant, not a discordant manner.
Furthermore, the subspecies category is often a
convenient shorthand for alluding to important
populations even when their genetic status is
ambiguous. What, for example, is the Florida panther?
It is a subspecies, a nearly vanished remnant of a series
of populations once widespread across the United
States, now further altered by hybridization with
panthers of South American origin released to the wild
in south Florida. Biologists rightly speak of the Florida
population in a way that calls attention to its genetic
distinctness, using one sharp phrase: the Florida
subspecies (or race, meaning the same thing) of Felis
concolor.
Soon afterward Brown and I made a second
conceptual discovery, this one unfettered by
controversy. We found a new phenomenon in
biodiversity, which we came to call character
displacement. The process is the exact opposite of
hybridization. In hybridization, two species exchange
genes where they meet, and as a result become overall
more similar. In character displacement two species
spring apart where they meet, like particles with the
same charge. I first encountered the mysterious effect
in the ant genus Lasius, which I had chosen as the
subject of my Ph.D. dissertation. During our lunchtime
dialogues Brown and I explored the possible causes and
searched the literature for a similar pattern in other
kinds of organisms.
We learned that the British ornithologist David
Lack had already delineated character displacement in
his 1947 study of Darwin’s finches on the Galápagos
Islands. In the 1970s and 1980s Peter Grant of
Princeton University, his wife, Rosemary, and their
students were to work out displacement in exquisite
detail through a lengthy field study of the same finches
in the Galápagos. Thus this little group of birds has
been favored by three of the best field studies in the
history of evolutionary biology: those by Darwin, Lack,
and the Grants, respectively. The principal contribution
that Brown and I made in our 1956 report was to show
that the repellant effect is widespread among animals
and is caused, according to the species pair considered,
by either competition or the active avoidance of
hybridization.

reading-4.title: Passage Iv
reading-4.html:
INFORMATIONAL: This passage is from the article “On the Rise: Victor Quijada” by Linde Howe-Beck (©2007 by Dance Media Publications, LLC).

A marvel of speed, precision, and invention,
Victor Quijada is riveting as a performer. His
movements coil tight and strong in the solar plexus,
leaving the upper back and limbs free. As artistic
director/choreographer of Montreal’s Rubberbandance
Group, he mixes hip hop with contemporary and
classical dance in a speedy, über-physical hybrid that
blends easy elegance with male-female confrontations
that threaten to become pileups. When he’s finished,
the audience is whooping.
Quijada’s movement is exhilarating and his
charisma is magnetic. Juxtaposing the raw freedom of
popping with concert dance’s technique and narrative,
Quijada’s pieces have unexpected moments of
tenderness and humor. But not everything about
Rubberbandance Group works perfectly, yet. Quijada is
a man with conflicting street-to-ballet impulses and he
is still the best interpreter of his own ideas, so he
continues to seek fresh ways to teach his dancers. “The
work that I’ve done has been cracking open the
potential of fusing hip hop energy with contemporary
aesthetics,” he says.
Quijada’s contemporary dance and ballet
credentials give him an unusual edge. A former Los
Angeles B-boy, he took to the streets at the age of 8
and later challenged the status quo in clubs, festivals,
or wherever break dancers met. After two years with
the Rudy Perez Performance Ensemble in Los Angeles,
he joined Twyla Tharp Dance for three years and then
relocated to Montreal to perform with Les Grands
Ballets Canadiens de Montréal.
His transition from street to studio was tough.
Along the way, he discovered he was opinionated and
undisciplined, as well as talented. He’d barely
graduated from the Los Angeles County High School
for the Arts when Tharp beckoned, launching his
biggest learning experience to date. Since he was the
only member of that company without ballet training,
he had to educate body and mind—fast.
Quijada is accustomed to adjusting. He’s spent
most of his 29 years tilting at tradition, first as the son
of Mexican immigrants. As he grew up, his need to
dance meant sharing sidewalks with his neighborhood’s
champion movers. Then he had to find his way as a
B-boy among contemporary and ballet dancers, and as
a classical dancer among break dancers. Stalked by a
sense of never fitting in, he began appraising all forms
of dance with a critical air. He assiduously searches out
and watches dance performances of every variety. As
with his own works, he is rarely satisfied. “I was—and
am—inspired by the lack of good dance,” he says
boldly.
In 2002, he founded Montreal’s Rubberbandance
Group with seven hip hop artists and ballet dancers.
First experiments were awkward because neither set of
dancers understood the other. Nevertheless they were
so different that choreographer and company got
instant attention from critics and public.
Quijada’s experiments won two United Kingdom
awards the following year. Rubberbandance has since
appeared in festivals in Toronto, New York,
Washington, Brussels, London, Helsinki, and Aichi,
Japan. Quijada choreographs for film and television
and has made pieces for Scottish Dance Theatre, New
York’s Chamber Dance Project, and Peter Boal and
Company.
One of Quijada’s challenges as a choreographer is
finding crossover dancers who can perform his
synthesis of styles. “I imagine having a company where
there are teams of different kinds of dancers. Ten years
from now I want the majority to be able to do
everything as well as having a few specialists—
breakers and ballet dancers,” says Quijada. Meanwhile,
he tries every possible combination. Currently
Rubberbandance numbers four (plus a part-timer)
including Quijada, Joseph Aurelien, Alexandra
Damiani, and Anne Plamondon.
Plamondon is the only dancer who has performed
Quijada’s choreography in pointe shoes, but she
forecasts that as dancers become accustomed to his
style, he will integrate more pointe work into frenetic
hip hop moves.

Scientists conducted a study to examine the effects of mixtures of vermicompost (feces from earthworms) and a particular potting soil on the growth of a certain species of tomato plant. Table 1 shows the compositions of vermicompost and potting soil (in percent by volume) for each of the 6 different mixtures (Mixtures K−P) that were used in the study.

science-3.title: Passage Iii
science-3.html:
Heliconia metallica is a plant found in the understory of tropical rain forests. (The understory is the area below the forest canopy.) H. metallica flowers are normally pollinated by hummingbirds. The flowers can be self-pollinated (egg and pollen are from the same H. metallica plant) or cross-pollinated (egg and pollen are from different H. metallica plants). The following study was conducted to investigate the effects of different pollination treatments on fruit production and seed mass in a population of H. metallica.

Study

Before pollination could occur, the anthers (pollen-producing structures) were removed from each of 400 H. metallica flowers. Then, the flowers were covered with nylon bags to prevent the normal pollinators from pollinating the flowers. The covered flowers were divided equally into 4 groups (Groups 1−4), and each group received a different pollination treatment (see Table 1). Four weeks after the pollination treatments, the percent of flowers that produced fruit and the average mass per seed were determined for each group (see Figures 1 and 2, respectively).

Table and figures adapted from Matthias Schleuning et al., “Effects of Inbreeding, Outbreeding, and Supplemental Pollen on the Reproduction of a Hummingbird-pollinated Clonal Amazonian Herb.” ©2010 by The Author(s).

science-4.title: Passage Iv
science-4.html:
Water that flows through underground aquifers (layers of permeable rock that serve as underground reservoirs) sometimes contains undesirable amounts of the elements arsenic (As) and antimony (Sb). Scientists studied how the amounts of As and Sb in groundwater from 2 coastal plain aquifers (Aquifers 1 and 2) varied along their known groundwater flow paths. The aquifers were unrelated.

Study

Aquifer 1 consisted of carbonate rock layers, while Aquifer 2 consisted of unconsolidated quartz sand. Within each aquifer, groundwater samples were taken from existing wells along known flow paths at various distances from the aquifer’s recharge zone (area where precipitation and surface runoff enters the underground aquifer). For Aquifer 1, 11 wells were sampled; for Aquifer 2, 6 wells were sampled. Prior to sample collection, all collection containers were rigorously cleaned. For each well, a 500 mL sample of groundwater was collected and immediately passed through a filter into its own sample bottle. A 60 mL portion of the filtered sample was then removed and analyzed for As and Sb. As and Sb contents were both measured in nanomoles per kilogram (nmol/kg).

The results for Aquifer 1 are shown in Figures 1 and 2, and the results for Aquifer 2 are shown in Figures 3 and 4.

Figures adapted from the article “Arsenic and Antimony in Groundwater Flow Systems: A Comparative Study” by Stephanie S. Willis, Shama E. Haque, and Karen H. Johannesson. (©2011 Springer Science+Business Media B. V.).

science-5.title: Passage V

Across 3 experiments, the relationships among pressure, volume, and temperature were investigated using samples of nitrogen gas (N2).

Experiment 1

A syringe, an N2 tank, and a pressure sensor were each connected to different ports of a 3-way valve (see Figure 1).

The valve was set so that N2 could flow from the tank into the syringe until the syringe was filled with 10 mL of N2 at a temperature of 298 kelvins (K). The valve was then set so that the pressure sensor could measure the pressure, in kilopascals (kPa), of the N2 in the syringe. The tank was then removed. The volume of the syringe was then adjusted to 3 other values without changing the temperature of the sample. The pressure was measured at each volume (see Table 1).

Experiment 2

The N2 tank was connected to one neck of a 2-necked rigid glass flask (see Figure 2).

With the stopper removed, N2 was allowed to flow through the flask for 5 min. At 5 min, the other neck of the flask was sealed with the stopper that was connected to a pressure sensor, and simultaneously a valve on the tank was closed. Then, in each of 4 trials, the flask was immersed in a water bath maintained at a particular temperature, left in the bath for 5 min, and then the pressure in the flask was measured (see Table 2).

Experiment 3

A balloon was filled with N2 from the tank and then sealed. In each of 4 trials, the volume of the balloon was measured while the balloon was held inside a chamber that was maintained at a pressure of 102 kPa and a particular temperature (see Table 3).

A voltmeter is a device used to measure voltage and contains 2 components, the meter itself (VM) and an internal resistor (RV) that resists the flow of electric current. A student conducted 2 studies using the circuit shown in Figure 1. In addition to the voltmeter, the circuit contained a 9-volt battery and 2 other resistors, R1 and R2.

Study 1

In each of 10 trials, the student first selected 3 resistors—each having a known resistance—for use as R1, R2, and RV and then connected them with copper wire to the voltmeter and a fresh battery. Upon connection, the voltmeter displayed the voltage across R2, which the student recorded. Table 1 lists, for each trial, the resistance (in kilohms, kΩ) of each of R1, R2, and RV and the voltage (in volts, V) across R2.

Study 2

The student repeated Trial 1 four times and combined the results with those of Study 1 to determine an average voltage across R2. She then used Ohm’s law and the loop and junction rules to calculate what the voltage across R2 would have been in the absence of a voltmeter. The student then performed this procedure for each of Trials 4, 8, and 10 (see Table 2).

science-7.title: Passage Vii
science-7.html:
Distillation is a method for separating compounds based on their boiling points (BPs). Figure 1 shows a distillation apparatus consisting of a distilling flask (DF), a distilling column (DC), a distilling head (DH), a thermometer, a condenser, and a collection flask (CF). The DF contains a 1:1 ethanol/H2O mixture by volume. Ethanol has a BP of 78.4°C and H2O has a BP of 100.0°C at 1 atmosphere (atm). Each of 4 students (Students 1−4) gave their opinions on how the distillation would proceed when the mixture was heated.

Student 1

Ethanol and H2O are far apart in BP, so they can be separated by distillation. The mixture will boil at 78.4°C, the BP of ethanol. The vapor will be pure ethanol at 78.4°C, which will condense and collect in the CF. When all the ethanol has distilled, the liquid remaining in the DF will boil at 100°C. The vapor will be pure H2O at 100°C, and will condense and collect in the CF.

Student 2

Student 1 is incorrect. Ethanol and H2O are too close in BP to be separated by distillation. The mixture will boil at 89.2°C, halfway between the BPs of the ethanol and H2O. The vapor will have the same composition as the mixture and will be at 89.2°C. It will condense into the same ethanol/H2O mixture and collect in the CF.

Student 3

Ethanol and H2O are close in BP but can be separated by distillation. The mixture will boil at 81.7°C. Ethanol has a lower BP than H2O, so the vapor will contain more ethanol than water. This vapor will condense and revaporize many times as it moves up the DC, becoming enriched in ethanol. The vapor that reaches the condenser first will be 100% ethanol at 78.4°C, and will condense and collect in the CF. As more of the mixture in the DF vaporizes, the amount of H2O in the vapor will increase and so will the proportion of H2O in the liquid that collects in the CF.

Student 4

Student 3 is correct except ethanol and H2O can only be partially separated by distillation. The vapor that reaches the condenser first and collects in the CF will be 96% ethanol and 4% H2O, the ethanol/H2O azeotrope (a mixture of 2 liquids that boils at a lower temperature than either liquid alone), at 78.1°C.
